outcomes.quiet: Little or no organized opposition found

sites.name: Project Blue
sites.end_user: Amazon Web Services, per public records; never publicly confirmed
sites.start_note: Pima County under a non-disclosure agreement from at least June 2024
sites.summary: Tucson's council unanimously refused to bring the campus into the city.
sites.history: Beale Infrastructure planned a 290-acre campus of up to 10 buildings, reported at 600 MW, that needed annexation into Tucson for city water. Records obtained by Arizona Luminaria named Amazon Web Services as the end user. The site would have cooled with drinking water for at least two years before switching to treated wastewater, in a region under long drought. Residents organized as No Desert Data Center, angered also that Pima County had sold land to the developer before any public meeting. On 6 August 2025 the city council voted unanimously against the project and began work on a data-center ordinance.
timeline: Pima County officials under a non-disclosure agreement
Tucson City Council votes unanimously against the project
Council begins work on a data-center ordinance
objections: Drinking water used for cooling in a drought
sites.case_for: The developer called the vote a missed opportunity for tax revenue, infrastructure and jobs, and said it had tried to earn trust by taking part in the city’s public meetings.
sites.after: A council member said the developers still intended to build somewhere in the region; nothing firm has been reported.

sites.name: Project Flo (Google)
sites.developer: Deep Meadows LLC, a Google affiliate
sites.summary: Google withdrew its rezoning request just before a council vote it was expected to lose.
sites.history: A Google affiliate asked to rezone 468 acres along I-74 for four data-center buildings, with ten years of tax cuts. Google was confirmed as the backer in July 2025, and the Metropolitan Development Commission approved the plan 8–1 in August. Opposition grew over the environment and secrecy: a council member had signed a non-disclosure agreement, and residents got a comment period instead of the public hearing they asked for. Facing a council majority against it, Google withdrew on 22 September 2025.
timeline: Rezoning proposal filed
Google confirmed as the company behind it
Metropolitan Development Commission approves, 8–1
Google withdraws before the council vote
objections: Secrecy, including a council member's NDA
sites.case_for: Google said it was disappointed the project would not go ahead.
sites.after: Organizers said they would stay alert, since Google could refile after three months.

sites.name: Project Aggie
sites.developer: Priority Power Management (backed by I Squared Capital)
sites.summary: The council unanimously refused to sell city land for the campus.
sites.history: Priority Power Management offered $30 million for about 200 acres of city-owned land in the Midtown Business Park, for a campus that could reach 600 MW with two 300 MW substations. City staff recommended the sale. More than 75 people signed up to speak and a petition gathered over 5,000 signatures, citing noise, the environment, demand on utilities and the process. On 11 September 2025 the council voted unanimously against the sale.
timeline: Residents push back against the land sale
Council votes unanimously against selling the land
sites.case_for: City staff recommended approving the $30 million sale.

sites.name: Harper Road Technology Park
sites.summary: The town removed data centers from its zoning code, ending a $1.5 billion plan.
sites.history: Diode Ventures planned up to seven 300,000 sq ft buildings on 504 acres next to a new Evergy substation, after the town added data centers to its light-industrial zoning. Opposition grew fast: a Facebook group reached about 1,000 members, roughly one in six local residents, and "No Hyperscale Data Centers" signs filled the aldermen's meetings. On 21 October 2024 the Board of Aldermen reversed itself and removed data centers from the code. The mayor, who backed the project, said the Kansas City Area Development Council had made clear the fight damaged the city's reputation.
timeline: Mayor reveals the plans
Planning commission proposes removing data centers from the zoning code
Board of Aldermen removes data centers from the code
objections: Scale of a hyperscale campus in a small town
sites.case_for: The mayor supported the project and called opponents "boisterous and ill-informed".
sites.after: Diode said it had no active application under the town's extended moratorium.

sites.name: Project Cumulus
sites.summary: The developer withdrew, and the city then paused all data-center projects for a year.
sites.history: CRG proposed an AI data center on 440 acres off Highway 370 for an end user its lawyer would only call a Fortune 100 company; city officials had signed non-disclosure agreements. Residents turned out to meeting after meeting over energy use, water quality and secrecy. CRG withdrew its permit application before the council's August 2025 vote, saying it would work with the city on a revised proposal, and the council then passed a one-year moratorium on data centers. The mayor said: "There's not enough transparency, and it turned into a lack of public trust."
timeline: Residents repeatedly pack public meetings
CRG withdraws before the council vote
Council approves a one-year pause on data-center projects
objections: Unnamed end user and officials' NDAs
sites.case_for: CRG said it withdrew to incorporate community feedback and would work on a revised proposal.
sources: KBIA / St. Louis Public Radio, Aug 2025

sites.name: Balico gas-powered campus
sites.mw_note: first phase of IT load; with a planned 3.5 GW gas plant
sites.summary: Supervisors rejected a data-center campus with its own 3.5 GW gas plant.
sites.history: Balico proposed data centers powered by an on-site 3.5 GW gas plant fed by the Mountain Valley Pipeline, first across about 2,200 acres and then, after resident opposition, on about 750. A study commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center estimated the plant would emit at least 326 tons of fine particles a year and add up to $48 million in health costs by 2040. Balico said the plant would meet all air-quality rules. On 15 April 2025 the Board of Supervisors voted 6–1 to reject the rezoning, which Balico had already said it would withdraw.
timeline: Plans revealed; first version withdrawn after opposition
Revised application filed: 12 buildings, 300 MW first phase
Supervisors reject the rezoning, 6–1
objections: Air pollution from the gas plant
sites.case_for: Balico said the plant would comply with federal and state air-quality rules.
sites.after: Balico said it was considering housing on the land instead.

sites.name: Provident campus
sites.summary: Withdrawn within weeks after residents and the town council objected.
sites.history: Provident Realty Advisors announced a $1.3 billion campus of eight 150,000 sq ft buildings on about 200 acres, aimed at a hyperscale tenant. Residents raised air, water, energy, wetland and wildlife concerns and worried about home values. Town council members said they could never support a project of that size in that place. Provident told the town on 10 June 2024 that it was withdrawing.
timeline: Campus announced
Provident withdraws the proposal
sites.case_for: Provident offered landscaped buffers and generator noise limits of 42 decibels.

sites.name: Chicago Trail campus
sites.place: near New Carlisle, St. Joseph County
sites.summary: Next to Amazon's campus, a second giant proposal was voted down 7–2.
sites.history: A developer sought to rezone about 1,000 acres of farmland along Chicago Trail for 14 buildings, reported as a $12 billion project, near the campus Amazon was building. The county plan commission voted unanimously against it in September 2025 and the New Carlisle town council filed a resolution opposing it. The developer and its backers, who included the county Republican chair and the commissioners' president, argued it would replace property-tax revenue lost to state cuts, with TV ads and door-to-door canvassing. After an eight-hour meeting that ended around 4 a.m. on 10 December 2025, the county council rejected the rezoning 7–2.
timeline: Area Plan Commission votes unanimously against
New Carlisle town council resolution opposing the rezoning
County council rejects the rezoning, 7–2
objections: Loss of farmland and rural character
sites.case_for: Property-tax revenue to offset state cuts, argued by the developer and backers including the county Republican chair and the commissioners' president.

sites.name: Archbald 1
sites.summary: One of several proposals in a small borough; council denied this 18-building plan.
sites.history: Five data-center projects across six sites were announced in Archbald, a borough in Lackawanna County, during 2025. Provident's application for an 18-building cluster became the focus: residents raised noise, light and air pollution, property values, wildlife habitat and water and power demand, and in March 2026 council members replaced the council's leaders, saying they weren't acting in residents' interest on the data centers. A hearing was canceled over a newspaper printing error, and on 27 March 2026 the council voted the application down at a special meeting attended by about 200 people.
timeline: Provident files a 22-building application across two sites
Council passes new data-center zoning rules, 5–2
Council changes its president
Council denies the 18-building application
sites.case_for: The developer described itself as a good neighbor; residents disputed that.
sites.after: Provident's earlier October 2025 application, which did not need a special vote, and other proposals in the borough are unresolved.

sites.name: Saturn business park
sites.start_note: residents learned of it; discussed with the city since 2024
sites.summary: The council rejected it, then voters banned data centers permanently.
sites.history: A 247,000 sq ft data center was proposed for a largely empty business park, hundreds of feet from homes, after discussions with the city since 2024. Residents said they had only recently learned of it and packed hearings over electricity, water, noise and air pollution; reports said it would use about three times the electricity of the whole city of 60,000. The council considered a moratorium in January 2026 and then rejected the project. To stop future councils reversing course, residents put a permanent ban on the June 2026 ballot, and more than 86% voted for it.
timeline: Council considers a moratorium
Council rejects the project
Voters approve a permanent ban, over 86% in favor
objections: Noise and air pollution near homes
sites.after: First voter-enacted permanent ban on data centers in the US, according to reports.
sources: AP via Anchorage Daily News, Jun 2026

sites.name: Stargate Michigan
sites.summary: The township voted no, was sued, and settled within weeks; construction began.
sites.history: Related Digital asked to rezone 575 acres of farmland for a data-center campus to be supplied with about 1.4 GW by DTE. In September 2025 the planning commission recommended against it and the township board voted 4–1 to deny it. Related and the landowners sued on 12 September alleging exclusionary zoning, and the township settled; a consent judgment was filed on 15 October 2025 with about $14 million in community benefits. The site was later announced as an OpenAI–Oracle Stargate campus and groundbreaking followed in November.
timeline: Planning commission and township board (4–1) reject the rezoning
Developer and landowners sue the township
Consent judgment filed: the project can proceed
Groundbreaking
Judge rejects a neighbor's challenge to the settlement
objections: A settlement that let the project proceed after the board voted no
sites.case_for: About $14 million in community benefits, including $4 million for farmland preservation; two-thirds of the wider 1,000-acre campus kept as open space, according to Oracle.
sites.after: Residents filed appeals and started a recall effort against three board members; construction continues.

sites.name: Lighthouse (Stargate)
sites.mw_note: four buildings; up to 3.5 GW at full build-out per Clean Wisconsin
sites.summary: Approved unanimously by the council; voters later demanded a say on big incentives.
sites.history: Vantage's $15 billion Lake Michigan campus was announced as an OpenAI–Oracle Stargate site in October 2025, with four buildings expected to need 1.3 GW. On 4 November 2025 the council unanimously created a tax increment district to repay Vantage's estimated $175 million of public infrastructure, at a meeting moved to a hotel banquet hall for the crowd. Opponents, led by Great Lakes Neighbors United, cited the speed and lack of input, a proposed transmission line, and Clean Wisconsin's estimate of large off-site water use for power generation. They launched a recall of the mayor, and in April 2026 about two-thirds of voters approved requiring a public vote on incentives above $10 million.
timeline: Announced as a Stargate site
Council creates the tax increment district, unanimously
Recall effort against the mayor
Referendum: voter approval needed for incentives over $10 million
objections: Water used to generate the power
sites.case_for: Vantage projects over 4,000 construction jobs and about 330 permanent staff, with about 700 jobs for the tenants, and pays upfront for water, sewer, roads and power infrastructure.

sites.name: Hyperion (Meta)
sites.developer: Meta, in a joint venture managed by Blue Owl
sites.mw_note: about 2 GW by 2030; up to 5 GW planned
sites.summary: Regulators approved three new gas plants to power Meta's largest data center.
sites.history: Meta announced a data center in rural Richland Parish in December 2024 at over $10 billion; by July 2026 it had raised the planned investment to more than $50 billion for a campus of about 2,250 acres that could reach 5 GW. To power it, Entergy Louisiana proposed three new gas plants and transmission lines. Consumer advocates warned of higher bills after Meta's 15-year contract and of relying on a non-public contract between two corporations; residents raised climate and water concerns. In August 2025 the Public Service Commission approved the plan 4–1.
timeline: Meta announces the campus
Public Service Commission approves Entergy's gas plants, 4–1
Blue Owl joint venture to finance at least $27 billion
Meta raises planned investment to more than $50 billion
objections: Climate impact of new gas plants
Jobs not guaranteed to local people
sites.case_for: Meta pays all the new plants' costs for 15 years, though not the transmission line; Entergy put the net bill impact at “plus or minus a dollar or so” a month to start.
sites.after: Under construction. Residents have complained about construction traffic and outages; Entergy denies the project harms the grid.

sites.name: Colossus (xAI)
sites.mw_note: 150 MW grid connection plus on-site gas turbines; SELC counted 35 turbines rated 422 MW
sites.summary: Built fast in a former factory, run partly on gas turbines; the permit came later.
sites.history: xAI turned a former Electrolux factory in Memphis into the Colossus AI supercomputer, online in July 2024, powered partly by temporary gas turbines. The Southern Environmental Law Center's aerial photos showed 35 turbines capable of 422 MW, while it said only 15 were permitted; groups including Memphis Communities Against Pollution opposed them over air quality. Some turbines were removed in May 2025 as a new 150 MW substation came online. On 2 July 2025 the Shelby County Health Department permitted 15 permanent turbines; the NAACP and others appealed.
timeline: Colossus comes online in a former Electrolux factory
Some turbines removed as a 150 MW substation connects
County permits 15 permanent turbines
NAACP and others appeal the permit
objections: Air pollution from turbines that opponents said were running without permits
A neighborhood already burdened by industry
sites.case_for: The city said air tests found no dangerous pollutant levels; xAI said its controls make it the lowest-emitting facility of its kind.
sites.after: xAI bought a second site in the Whitehaven area in 2025.

sites.name: Project Marvel
sites.mw_note: full capacity, per the developer's law firm
sites.summary: Rezoned 5–2 over near-unanimous opposition in the room.
sites.history: Logistic Land Investments proposed 18 buildings totalling 4.5 million sq ft on about 700 mostly wooded acres, a $14.5 billion project with no tenant yet. The developer's lawyers put it at about 1,200 MW, and reporting said it could raise Alabama's electricity demand by up to 10%. Neighbors sued in April 2025 to make the city disclose what council members reviewed before voting; critics said officials who signed non-disclosure agreements weren't open with the public. Residents wearing red packed the November 2025 meeting over water, power, 300 to 500 diesel backup generators and an imperiled fish on the site, the Birmingham darter. The council approved the rezoning 5–2.
timeline: Neighbors sue for disclosure
Council approves the rezoning, 5–2
Disclosure lawsuit dismissed by agreement of both sides
sites.case_for: Supporters, including the school superintendent, pointed to tax revenue; the developer said there would be no power-rate increases, which a council member said it was in no position to promise.
sites.after: Project under way.

sites.name: Project Sail
sites.summary: Commissioners approved a 900 MW campus 15 months after it was proposed.
sites.history: Atlas Development proposed a nine-building, 4.3 million sq ft campus on about 830 acres near Newnan in January 2025, and the logistics company Prologis later moved to buy the site. Residents argued it would strain the area's resources; a Facebook group of about 4,800 members discussed legal action and a fundraiser raised about $27,000 for lawyers. In April 2026 the county commissioners approved the rezoning 3–2.
timeline: Atlas files the proposal
Reports that Prologis will buy the site
Commissioners approve the rezoning, 3–2
sites.after: Opponents were raising money for a possible legal challenge.

sites.name: Farmington Technology Park
sites.summary: Approved; residents sued, then dropped the suit over legal costs. A township's suit continues.
sites.history: Tract plans up to 12 buildings and 2.5 million sq ft on 340 acres, about $5 billion at full build-out. Residents formed the Coalition for Responsible Data Center Development, more than 350 members, and sued in November 2024 over air, noise, water and power use and building heights. The council approved the final plan in December 2024, and neighboring Castle Rock Township sued in January 2025 saying the city broke an annexation agreement. In September 2026 the coalition dropped its suit because a few residents could no longer carry the cost.
timeline: Castle Rock Township asks the Metropolitan Council to deny the rezoning
Residents' coalition sues
Council approves the final plan
Castle Rock Township votes to sue
Coalition withdraws its suit, citing legal costs
objections: Power demand and who pays for infrastructure
sites.case_for: Tract says the planning commission and council each approved by large majorities, twice.
sites.after: The township's lawsuit is unaffected by the coalition's withdrawal.

sites.name: PW Digital Gateway
sites.developer: QTS and Compass Datacenters (as H&H Capital Acquisitions and GW Acquisition Co.)
sites.summary: A 2,100-acre rezoning beside a Civil War battlefield was approved, then voided by the courts.
sites.history: In December 2023, after a 29-hour public hearing, Prince William's supervisors narrowly rezoned about 2,100 acres beside Manassas National Battlefield Park for 23 million sq ft of data centers. Neighbors in the Oak Valley Homeowners Association and the American Battlefield Trust sued. In August 2025 a circuit judge voided the rezoning, ruling that the county had not given proper public notice, and the Court of Appeals upheld that on 31 March 2026. The county then dropped its defense and Compass stepped back; QTS appealed to the Supreme Court of Virginia, which could decide whether to hear it from autumn 2026.
timeline: Supervisors approve the rezoning after a 29-hour hearing
Circuit court voids the rezoning over public notice
Builders barred from starting while appeals continue
Court of Appeals upholds the ruling
County withdraws from the appeals
Compass says it won't appeal
QTS appeals to the Supreme Court of Virginia
objections: Next to a Civil War battlefield
Public notice the court found inadequate
sites.case_for: The county board approved it in 2023 and spent about $1.7 million defending it before withdrawing.
sites.after: If the Supreme Court takes the case, a final ruling could come around mid-2027.

sites.name: Amazon Warrenton
sites.summary: Approved in 2023, then stalled for three years in court.
sites.history: Amazon bought a 42-acre site on Blackwell Road and applied to build a single-story, 220,000 sq ft data center in this small Virginia town. The town council granted a special use permit in February 2023 over local opposition, and Citizens for Fauquier County and residents sued, arguing the 2021 zoning change that first allowed data centers was void. The council removed data centers as a permitted use in July 2025, which did not cancel Amazon's permit. Trial began in March 2026 with a final hearing set for June, while construction has not started.
timeline: Amazon applies; planners pause the hearing in November for missing studies
Town council grants a special use permit
Residents and Citizens for Fauquier County sue
Council removes data centers as a permitted use, 6–0
Trial begins; final hearing set for 15 June 2026
Final hearing held; no ruling reported yet
objections: How the 2021 zoning change was made
sites.case_for: Amazon argues the permit was a separate, publicly vetted decision and that no one knew of any problem with the zoning amendment.
sites.after: The final hearing took place in June 2026. As of 18 October 2026 we have not found a reported ruling.

sites.name: Stargate Abilene
sites.developer: Stargate (OpenAI and Oracle with their investors)
sites.summary: Two people spoke at the meeting that approved its tax break; concerns came later.
sites.history: The first Stargate campus began quietly in June 2024: eight buildings, 4 million sq ft on 1,100 acres, eventually drawing about 1.2 GW, with an on-site gas plant. At a sparsely attended special meeting in February 2025 the city council unanimously approved an 85% property-tax abatement; only one resident spoke against it. Two buildings were running by early 2026. Concerns since have centered on construction traffic, gas-plant emissions, the size of the tax break and a housing crunch.
timeline: Work begins
Council unanimously approves the tax abatement
Two buildings operating
objections: Raised later: traffic, gas-plant emissions, tax abatement, housing costs
sites.case_for: An economic impact of up to $4 billion over two decades claimed by boosters; 357 full-time jobs required by the deal.

sites.name: Project Jade
sites.developer: Crusoe, with Tallgrass building the power plant
sites.summary: A 1.8 GW campus approved with only scattered objections.
sites.history: Crusoe and Tallgrass announced a 1.8 GW AI campus near the Colorado border, powered by an adjacent 2.7 GW gas-fired plant, which reports said would use more electricity than every home in Wyoming. Laramie County approved it in January 2026. A neighboring rancher objected to lights, dust and the changed landscape, and some residents asked about water; Crusoe said closed-loop cooling keeps water use minimal. We found no organized campaign against it.
timeline: Project announced
Laramie County approves the campus and power plant
objections: Individual objections: views, lights, dust, water
sites.case_for: Tallgrass cites $7 billion of energy infrastructure; total cost could reach $50 billion.

sites.name: AWS New Carlisle
sites.summary: An $11 billion campus that went ahead with state incentives and little early resistance.
sites.history: Amazon announced an $11 billion data-center campus in April 2024 inside the Indiana Enterprise Center, a planned industrial park of nearly 3,000 acres beside a town of about 1,600 people, with at least 1,000 jobs promised. The state offered performance-based tax credits and grants, and Amazon agreed to put up to $7 million toward roads. We found no organized opposition to it at the time. When a second giant campus was proposed nearby in 2025, opponents argued the area's rural character was already changing as Amazon built.
timeline: Amazon announces the campus
County rejects a second campus nearby
objections: None organized at the time found
sites.case_for: At least 1,000 jobs; state tax credits are claimable only after investment is made.

sites.name: Fairwater (Microsoft)
sites.summary: Built without an organized fight; neighbors sued over fan noise after it opened.
sites.history: Microsoft announced its Wisconsin data-center investment in May 2024 and finished the first Fairwater building in Mount Pleasant in 2026, calling it the world's most powerful AI supercomputer; a second building is due in 2028. We found no organized opposition before construction. In July 2026, three neighbors in Sturtevant filed a proposed class action saying the cooling fans' constant noise had invaded their homes, on behalf of more than 1,000 households within 1.5 miles.
timeline: Microsoft announces its Wisconsin investment
First building's equipment brought online
Neighbors file a class action over noise
sites.case_for: About 550 full-time staff at the first building and 10,000 construction workers over two years, per Microsoft; $4.7 billion of local construction spending estimated for 2024 to 2028.

sites.name: Project Nova (Microsoft)
sites.summary: Microsoft dropped the site after a local campaign, Stop Project Nova, days before a rezoning vote.
sites.history: Microsoft applied in August 2025 to rezone 244 acres west of We Energies' Oak Creek coal plant, with a 15-acre substation; its involvement became public in late September. Residents organized as Stop Project Nova, and about 30 people spoke against it at a September meeting. On 8 October 2025, ahead of a 14 October vote, Microsoft withdrew, citing community feedback, and said it would look for a site that "aligns with community priorities". At the same time it announced another $4 billion to double its campus in nearby Mount Pleasant.
timeline: Rezoning application submitted
Microsoft named; about 30 speak against at a meeting
Microsoft withdraws
objections: Community opposition organized as Stop Project Nova
sites.case_for: Microsoft said it remained committed to investing in southeast Wisconsin.
sites.after: Microsoft expanded its nearby Mount Pleasant campus instead.

sites.name: Francis Harris Lane
sites.summary: Turned down twice; the second time 5–2 at 2:14 in the morning.
sites.history: A Fort Worth developer sought to rezone about 200 acres next to the Hays Energy power plant, between San Marcos and New Braunfels, for a $1.5 billion data center. The planning commission recommended denial in March 2025 and a zoning change failed to reach the council supermajority it needed that summer. The developer returned with water-use concessions, but 182 people signed up to speak, most against, in a region in long drought. At 2:14 a.m. on 18 February 2026 the council voted 5–2 to deny the land-use change.
timeline: Planning and Zoning Commission recommends denial
Zoning change fails to get a council supermajority
Council denies the land-use change, 5–2
sites.case_for: Construction jobs lasting up to five years, backed by union workers, and city tax revenue; the developer offered water-use concessions.
sites.after: The developer can refile after six months. Hays County's judge proposed a moratorium on new water-intensive permits.

sites.name: Mooresville Technology Park
sites.summary: Tract withdrew a campus on land once owned by NASCAR's Dale Earnhardt.
sites.history: Tract sought to rezone 400 acres outside Mooresville, owned by Teresa Earnhardt, widow of the NASCAR driver, for 1.5 million sq ft of data centers that residents nicknamed the "Concrete Monster". About 200 residents protested over several meetings and set up a campaign website; Dale Earnhardt's son Kerry spoke against it. In August 2025 Tract withdrew fully before the council could discuss it, and the mayor said there was no active data-center request in the town.
timeline: Residents protest the rezoning over several meetings
Tract withdraws the plan

sites.name: Active Infrastructure campus
sites.summary: Rejected unanimously despite a former US senator lobbying for it.
sites.history: A New York developer proposed an AI data center on 40 acres near Queen Creek and Dobson roads in Chandler. Former Senator Kyrsten Sinema attended several city meetings urging approval, framing it as part of the national AI push. The city received over 250 emails against and 10 in favor. On 11 December 2025 the council voted 7–0 against it. The mayor said "almost-jobless buildings" did not fit the city's plans for its Price Road business corridor, home to Intel and Wells Fargo.
timeline: Former Sen. Sinema urges the council to advance it
Council rejects it, 7–0
objections: Few jobs for the land used
sites.case_for: Supporters, including former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema, tied it to national AI priorities.

sites.name: Balloonist campus
sites.summary: The mayor halted a $1.6 billion plan weeks after the city annexed the land for it.
sites.history: In August 2025 Menomonie annexed and rezoned about 320 acres of farmland for a $1.6 billion data center by Balloonist LLC, whose end user was never named; the city administrator had signed a non-disclosure agreement. Opposition grew across the city and region, much of it over secrecy. On 22 September 2025 the mayor announced he would not pursue a tax district or development agreement, calling it "not a suitable fit".
timeline: City annexes and rezones the land
Mayor puts the project on hold
sites.case_for: A city FAQ cited up to 1,000 construction jobs and 50 to 75 full-time jobs.
sites.after: The annexation and rezoning still stand; organizers expected possible legal action by the developer.

sites.name: Project Accelerate
sites.developer: Matthews DC LLC, with Crosland Southeast
sites.summary: Withdrawn a week before the rezoning hearing in a Charlotte suburb.
sites.history: Developers petitioned to rezone 123 acres along East John Street in Matthews, southeast of Charlotte, for a data center. Residents raised power demand, property taxes, noise and environmental impact. On 7 October 2025, ahead of a 13 October hearing, the mayor announced the petition had been withdrawn; the developer said it wanted more time to explore options.
timeline: Rezoning petition filed
Mayor announces the withdrawal

sites.name: Howell Township campus
sites.developer: Randee LLC and Stantec, on land owned by the Van Gilder family
sites.summary: A rezoning for more than 1,000 acres of farmland was pulled the night before the vote.
sites.history: Developers sought to rezone more than 1,000 acres, largely farmland owned by a local family, for a data center reportedly backed by Meta. In late November the township passed a data-center moratorium while it wrote rules; opponents said it did not cover this request. Stop the Data Centers Livingston County urged the board to keep to its master plan. On 7 December 2025, the night before the board was due to consider it, the request was withdrawn to honor the moratorium.
timeline: Township adopts a moratorium on data centers
Rezoning request withdrawn
objections: Farmland and the township master plan
sites.case_for: The landowning family said it had submitted the best proposal for the land.
sites.after: The township is drafting data-center rules; opponents expect the request to return.

sites.name: Aligned campus
sites.summary: East of Columbus, a city council turned down Aligned Data Centers unanimously.
sites.history: Aligned Data Centers proposed a campus in Pataskala, in Licking County east of Columbus; the planning and zoning commission voted 5–2 to deny it. Residents cited water, land, new substations and power lines, permanent noise and a four-story building. On 25 August 2026 the city council unanimously accepted the commission's recommendation.
timeline: Planning and Zoning Commission recommends denial, 5–2
Council rejects it unanimously
sites.after: A November ballot measure in the area concerns data centers over 25 MW.

sites.name: West Valley campus
sites.summary: A $14 billion park withdrawn after neighboring cities' planners objected.
sites.history: Tract applied to rezone about 1,000 acres in an unincorporated county island near Yuma and Perryville roads for up to 30 buildings and 5.6 million sq ft, a $14 billion project. Staff in Goodyear and Buckeye objected that it did not fit the land uses planned for the area. Tract withdrew the request in April 2024. Here the pushback came mainly from city planners rather than an organized residents' campaign.
timeline: Plan reported
Tract withdraws after Goodyear and Buckeye object
objections: Incompatible with planned land uses (city staff)

sites.name: Jones Road
sites.summary: A small 200,000 sq ft project caught as the county weighed a moratorium.
sites.history: County staff denied a 200,000 sq ft data center on Jones Road in June 2026, citing violations of the land-management ordinance, while the county council considered a moratorium. The developer appealed, saying the county had been positive until late June and that it had already invested over $28 million. In August 2026 the Board of Zoning Appeals unanimously upheld the denial.
timeline: County staff deny the application
Board of Zoning Appeals upholds the denial
objections: Residents asking for county rules first
sites.case_for: The developer said it had invested over $28 million on the county's earlier signals.
sites.after: The developer can reapply, though a county moratorium could block it.

sites.name: AWS third Louisa campus
sites.summary: After two by-right campuses, Amazon's third needed a public permit and was withdrawn.
sites.history: Amazon has invested $11 billion in two Louisa County campuses that were allowed by right. In 2024 the county shrank its technology zone and required a conditional use permit for new projects, and in May 2025 AWS applied for a third campus of up to 7.2 million sq ft and seven substations on 1,370 acres by the Northeast Creek Reservoir. Residents objected to light, noise, air quality, water, nearby schools and the pace of development; some felt betrayed by earlier approvals. AWS withdrew on 23 July 2025.
timeline: County requires a public permit for new data centers
AWS applies for a third campus
AWS withdraws
AWS buys about 1,920 acres near the reservoir for about $72 million
sites.case_for: A county supervisor pointed to tax revenue and jobs; AWS said it heard the community and wanted more input on future projects.
sites.after: Amazon later bought land near the reservoir, saying it was for water infrastructure; the board chair said he opposes any data center there.

sites.name: xAI Southaven power plant
sites.mw_note: power plant of about 1.2 GW, not a data center load
sites.summary: Temporary turbines ran for months without a permit, which regulators said they didn’t need; the state then approved 41 permanent ones.
sites.history: To power Colossus 2 across the state line in Memphis, an xAI affiliate set up temporary gas turbines at a plant it bought in Southaven, running from August 2025 without a permit; regulators said temporary-mobile units are exempt for up to a year. It then applied for 41 permanent turbines, about 1.2 GW; residents said the site is less than half a mile from their homes. Residents unanimously opposed it at a February 2026 hearing over noise and air pollution, and the NAACP and Southern Environmental Law Center gave notice of a Clean Air Act suit. On 10 March 2026 the state permit board approved it unanimously.
timeline: Temporary turbines begin running
NAACP gives notice of a Clean Air Act challenge
Public hearing; residents oppose
Permit board approves 41 turbines, unanimously
objections: Nitrogen oxides and particulates near homes
Turbines running before any permit was issued
A process opponents called rushed (short notice, hearing timing)
sites.case_for: Regulators said modeling showed the area would stay within national air-quality standards.
sites.after: Groups said they would pursue legal action.

sites.name: Homer City campus
sites.mw_note: 4.5 GW gas plant planned; data-center load not published
sites.summary: A coal town welcomed it; statewide environmental groups are appealing the gas plant.
sites.history: The former Homer City coal plant, once Pennsylvania's largest, is being turned into a 3,200-acre AI data-center campus powered by a 4.5 GW gas plant, with more than $10 billion of initial investment. Local business and labor leaders and the governor welcomed it. Statewide groups including PennFuture, Clean Air Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice objected to its emissions, which they said would be almost three times the CO2 of any other single plant in the state. The state approved the air plan on 18 November 2025, and the groups appealed in December.
timeline: Plan announced with Kiewit
State issues the air-quality plan approval
Environmental groups appeal to the Environmental Hearing Board
sites.case_for: About 10,000 construction jobs and around 1,000 permanent jobs claimed; local leaders said it would put the town on the map.
sites.after: The appeal is pending; power is targeted for 2027.

sites.name: Mason County campus
sites.developer: Maysville-Mason County Industrial Authority, for an unnamed company
sites.summary: Rezoned for an unnamed tech giant despite a 4,300-member opposition group.
sites.history: An anonymous developer surveyed land near the Ohio River in November 2025, and the county industrial authority proposed rezoning 2,080 acres across 28 properties for a campus reported at about 2.2 GW, for an unnamed Fortune 50 technology company. Residents formed a Facebook group of about 4,300 members, gathered more than 1,200 petition signatures and called for a moratorium. On 22 May 2026 the county fiscal court rezoned the land for rural industrial use.
timeline: Anonymous developer surveys land
Fiscal court rezones 2,080 acres
sites.case_for: The company would pay all electrical, water and road costs; up to 2,600 jobs, mostly in construction.

sites.name: Greenfield Road (CoreWeave)
sites.developer: Chirisa Technology Parks and Machine Investment Group
sites.summary: Approved by a zoning officer without a hearing; residents have been trying to reopen it since.
sites.history: CoreWeave committed $6 billion to data centers in two former printing plants in Lancaster. In February 2025 the city's zoning officer classed them as warehouses, a permitted use that needed no public hearing. The planning commission questioned that classification and held a hearing, saying the city had lost its chance to control the project, and planned to ask the council for data-center zoning rules. Construction began, and in September 2026 a residents' group, Lancaster Residents Against Glut and Exhaust, appealed the approval of a second building.
timeline: Zoning officer approves without a hearing
Planning commission hearing on the decision
Residents' group appeals the second building's approval
sites.case_for: The developer says the use is permitted and the appeal has no merit.
sites.after: The first building is under construction for 2027.

sites.name: Amazon Hobart
sites.summary: Approved with tax breaks before any site plan existed; a resident sued.
sites.history: In January 2026 Hobart's council approved an $11 billion Amazon project on hundreds of acres, designating it an economic revitalization area with a ten-year tax abatement and a long IT-equipment exemption, while Amazon paid the city $47 million with more payments tied to milestones. No site plan, renderings or environmental study had been released. A resident's group, No Data Centers Hobart Indiana, filed two lawsuits, arguing the land did not qualify for the abatement and that required steps were skipped, and sought to stop the soil-testing fill permit.
timeline: Council approves the project and tax breaks
Plan commission approves a fill permit; lawsuits filed
objections: No site plan or environmental study
Residents’ questions about Amazon’s influence on local decisions
sites.case_for: Amazon promises more than 400 permanent jobs averaging about $37 an hour; the mayor called it minimally impactful and economically beneficial.
sites.after: Amazon targets completion in 2028.

sites.name: Ridgeline
sites.mw_note: first-phase computing load; with 800 MW gas and 1.3 GW solar
sites.summary: An off-grid gas-and-solar complex in the mountains; its air permit survived appeal.
sites.history: Fundamental Data plans a 5 GW complex on 291 acres near Thomas: in its first phase, 800 MW of gas, 1.3 GW of solar and 14 data-center buildings with more than 2 GW of computing load, under the state's Power Generation and Consumption Act. The state issued the gas plant's air permit in August 2025. Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and Sierra Club appealed, but the Air Quality Board upheld the permit on 5 February 2026, and in August regulators found the developer had shown control of the site.
timeline: State issues the gas plant's air permit
Air Quality Board upholds the permit
Regulators find site control was satisfied
objections: Gas plant classified as a minor source
sites.case_for: The developer says users bear the power costs, it seeks no state or county money, and solar cuts gas use.
sites.after: Commercial operation is targeted for 2028.

sites.name: HyperGrid (Fermi America)
sites.developer: Fermi America, with Texas Tech University System
sites.mw_note: planned IT capacity; 1 GW targeted for 2026
sites.summary: An 11 GW plan on the Ogallala Aquifer, backed by a former energy secretary.
sites.history: Fermi America, co-founded by former Energy Secretary Rick Perry, is building a campus of about 6,000 acres outside Amarillo with Texas Tech, planned at 11 GW and powered by its own grid of gas, solar, wind and, eventually, nuclear reactors. Amarillo approved a water supply agreement in October 2025. Dozens of residents formed a coalition against it, calling it an existential threat to the Ogallala Aquifer; the city says there is enough water, and Fermi says closed-loop cooling uses little.
timeline: Fermi buys its first gas turbines
City approves a water supply agreement
First turbines delivered
objections: Residents’ doubts about the developer’s water figures
sites.case_for: Economic growth; the developer says closed-loop cooling needs little water.

sites.name: Amazon Birchwood campus
sites.summary: The county approved it, a new board reversed course, Amazon sued, and the county settled just before trial.
sites.history: Amazon bought the 869-acre former Birchwood power plant site for almost $169 million to build up to 17 data centers, up to $6 billion. The county approved the project in 2023 and a performance agreement on 19 December 2023, then reversed the agreement on 2 January 2024 under new officials who said Amazon's payments did not justify giving up the land, and began moves to downzone it. Amazon sued in April 2025 claiming vested rights. Before a trial set for late September 2026, the county settled: it accepted that Amazon has vested rights to build, Amazon agreed to pay $10 million toward a school building and not to put data centers beside the Rappahannock River, and the county gave up rezoning the whole site.
timeline: County approves the campus
Performance agreement approved
New board reverses the agreement
Amazon sues
County settles before trial; the project can proceed
objections: Payments too small to justify the land (the board, in 2024)
Some residents wanted the county to keep fighting
sites.case_for: Amazon pledges more than 100 jobs and $10 million toward a school building; the board chair said fighting on risked costly lawsuits and that Amazon could legally have built anyway.
sites.after: A water agreement, a final performance agreement and tax figures are still being negotiated. Amazon withdrew a state application to draw groundwater from the Potomac aquifer.

sites.name: Hermantown (Google)
sites.developer: not named; Google as end user
sites.summary: Revealed late, challenged in court, then scaled back; Google dropped its tax break request in October 2026.
sites.history: A large data-center project near Duluth became public in September 2025; according to the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy, records requests showed the city had known of it for over a year. A citizen petition paused it, and in November 2025 the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy and Stop the Hermantown Data Center sued over the environmental review. Google was revealed as the end user in March 2026 and agreed to a smaller footprint and a new review. The city granted a tax abatement worth up to $80 million in May 2026, but Google dropped the request on 14 October 2026.
timeline: Project revealed; environmental review comments
Environmental groups and residents sue
Google named; smaller footprint and new review
City grants up to $80 million in tax abatements
Google drops the tax abatement request
City council to decide the special use permit
objections: How long the project was kept from the public
sites.case_for: The city projects over $240 million in property taxes over 20 years.
sites.after: The planning and zoning commission hears Google's special use permit on 20 October 2026, and the city council decides it at a dedicated meeting on 26 October.

sites.name: Comanche Circle
sites.summary: Residents asked for a pause; commissioners refused 3–2 after a state senator's warning.
sites.history: Hood County has at least four proposed data centers. The largest, Comanche Circle, would put nine campuses totaling up to 5 GW on about 2,600 acres near the Comanche Peak nuclear plant, over a recharge zone of the Upper Trinity Aquifer. Residents pushed for a six-month moratorium to study water, power, air and noise. A state senator wrote that counties lack that power and asked the attorney general to investigate such pauses, and on 10 February 2026 commissioners rejected the moratorium 3–2.
timeline: Commissioners reject a six-month moratorium, 3–2
objections: Aquifer water, up to 1 million gallons a day at full build-out
sites.case_for: The Data Center Coalition cites jobs and tax revenue; a state senator said counties lack the legal power to pause development.

sites.name: Frontier (Vantage)
sites.summary: A $25 billion campus announced to a welcome from the county judge.
sites.history: Vantage announced Frontier in August 2025: ten buildings and 3.7 million sq ft on 1,200 acres in a rural county outside Abilene, 1.4 GW of AI capacity and more than $25 billion, its largest project. Construction had already begun, with the first building due in late 2026. The county judge and the governor welcomed it, and we found no reported local opposition.
timeline: Announced, with construction under way
sites.case_for: Jobs and education opportunities, per the county judge; closed-loop cooling with minimal water.

sites.name: Polaris Forge 1 (Applied Digital)
sites.start_note: first coverage of the AI campus
sites.summary: A town of 1,100 accepted it as a lifeline, with some worries.
sites.history: Applied Digital's campus outside Ellendale includes a bitcoin-mining facility and is adding AI buildings for CoreWeave under a lease worth about $7 billion over 15 years, with state approval for up to 530 MW. The mayor called it a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for a shrinking town. Some residents worried about brownouts, bills, noise and the town's identity, and one said she wished she'd known before buying her house, but we found no organized campaign against it.
timeline: AI buildings under construction beside the bitcoin site
CoreWeave lease announced
objections: Individual concerns: brownouts, bills, noise, town identity
sites.case_for: 300 to 350 jobs, new housing and a larger tax base after annexation.

opposition.note: Data Center Watch quarterly reports: at least 75 projects worth about $130 billion in Q1 2026 and 45 worth about $68 billion in Q2; 843 local groups in 49 states. Its methods are not published in detail, and a project can appear in more than one quarter.

tags.state-regulator: The decision that set the outcome was made by a state regulator or permit board, not a local government
tags.new-gas: New gas-fired power is being built for the project (its own plant or turbines, or utility plants dedicated to it)
tags.nda: Sources report local officials signed non-disclosure agreements about the project
tags.court: A lawsuit or formal appeal was filed by opponents or the developer
tags.withdrawn: The developer withdrew before a final vote
tags.ballot: Voters decided a measure prompted by the project
tags.anonymous: The end user was not publicly confirmed when the outcome was decided
